title: "I Remember That Question: Using Eye Tracking to See How Prequestions Shape Reading"

abstract: "Answering questions before learning (prequestions) improves memory for the information they address, but how it does so is unclear. A common proposal is that prequestions direct attention to that information. We tested this account by recording eye movements while participants read a text about polio and tuberculosis after answering prequestions about one topic or none, so that every target sentence was read both with and without prequestions. Prequestions improved memory only for the prequestioned information, and eye movements showed the same specificity. Ex-Gaussian models, which separate typical reading time from occasional unusually long readings, showed that prequestions did not change typical reading of the answer sentences. Instead, these sentences received more unusually long readings, were looked back to more often, and were re-read for longer; other sentences were unaffected. Prequestions thus guide attention selectively rather than heightening it, consistent with additional processing when readers recognize an answer."
keywords: [prequestions, pretesting, eye tracking, reading, attention, learning]

```{r}
  n <- nrow(tab)
  if (n == 0) return("")
  sprintf("%s %s %s and %s excluded.", str_to_sentence(n_word(n)),
          if (n == 1) "participant" else "participants", reason,
          if (n == 1) "was" else "were")

# BAYESIAN MODELS ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# Results of the three Bayesian analysis documents (analysis/prequestions.qmd,
# analysis/final_test.qmd, analysis/eye_tracking.qmd), combined: tables with the same
# name are stacked (they carry a `model` column); the rest are taken as they are
bayes <- local({
  r <- map(c("prequestions", "final_test", "eye_tracking"),
           \(x) readRDS(here::here("analysis", sprintf("results_%s.rds", x))))
  out <- list()
  for (x in r) for (nm in names(x)) {
    out[[nm]] <- if (is.data.frame(x[[nm]]) && !is.null(out[[nm]])) bind_rows(out[[nm]], x[[nm]])
                 else if (is.null(out[[nm]])) x[[nm]] else out[[nm]]
  }
  out
})
```

```{r}
#| label: bayes-helpers
#| include: false
# Posterior summaries for the text and tables. Durations were modelled in s/word and are
# reported in ms per word; probabilities and proportions in percent.
b_scale <- c(total_fix = 1000, first_pass = 1000, reread_time = 1000, regressed_in = 100,
             final_test = 100)
b_unit  <- c(total_fix = "ms per word", first_pass = "ms per word",
             reread_time = "ms per word", regressed_in = "percentage points",
             final_test = "percentage points")
est_col <- \(x) intersect(c("Mean", "Difference", "Probability", "Median"), names(x))[1]

# One comparison a - b: pooled models compare statuses ("Prequestioned",
# "Non-prequestioned", "Control"); within a topic (tp), the Condition x Topic models
# compare conditions ("Polio", "TB", "Control"). Comparisons saved the other way round
# are reversed.
BY_row <- function(mod, a, b = "Control", par = "mu") {
  e <- filter(bayes$est, model == mod, parameter == par)
  sgn <- 1
  r <- filter(e, Level1 == a, Level2 == b)
  if (nrow(r) == 0) {
    r <- filter(e, Level1 == b, Level2 == a)
    sgn <- -1
  }
  f <- filter(bayes$bf, model == mod, parameter == par,
              comparison == paste(r$Level1, "-", r$Level2))
  stopifnot(nrow(r) == 1, nrow(f) == 1)
  k <- sgn * (if (par == "hu") 100 else b_scale[[mod]])
  tibble(est = k * r[[est_col(r)]], lo = min(k * r$CI_low, k * r$CI_high),
         hi = max(k * r$CI_low, k * r$CI_high), pd = r$pd, BF10 = f$BF10, BF01 = f$BF01)
}
# Group x Topic models: Polio - TB within a group ("Polio", "TB", "Control"), or the
# interaction contrast ("Interaction": the Polio group's Polio - TB minus the TB group's)
gt_lab <- \(grp) if (grp == "Interaction") "Interaction (Polio group - TB group)" else
  paste0("Polio - TB (", grp, " group)")
GT_row <- function(mod, grp, par = "mu") {
  e <- filter(bayes$est_topic, model == mod, parameter == par, comparison == gt_lab(grp))
  f <- filter(bayes$bf_topic, model == mod, parameter == par, comparison == gt_lab(grp))
  stopifnot(nrow(e) == 1, nrow(f) == 1)
  k <- if (par == "hu") 100 else b_scale[[mod]]
  tibble(est = k * e$Mean, lo = k * e$CI_low, hi = k * e$CI_high, pd = e$pd,
         BF10 = f$BF10, BF01 = f$BF01)
}
# Predicted sign of Polio - TB: positive in the Polio group and for the interaction,
# negative in the TB group (no prediction for Control)
gt_sign <- c(Polio = 1, TB = -1, Interaction = 1)
GT_pos <- \(mod, grp, par = "mu") { r <- GT_row(mod, grp, par); gt_sign[[grp]] * r$est > 0 && r$pd > 0.95 }
fmt_BF <- function(bf) {
  if (bf >= 1000) {
    e <- floor(log10(bf))
    sprintf("%s × 10^%d^", fmt_num(bf / 10^e, 1), e)
  } else if (bf >= 100) fmt_num(bf, 0) else fmt_num(bf, 2)
}
# BF10 when the evidence favours a difference, BF01 when it favours none
bf_txt <- \(r) if (r$BF10 >= 1) paste("BF~10~ =", fmt_BF(r$BF10)) else paste("BF~01~ =", fmt_BF(r$BF01))
pd_txt <- \(pd) if (pd >= 0.9995) "pd > 99.9%" else paste0("pd = ", fmt_num(100 * pd, 1), "%")
row_txt <- function(r, unit) {
  sprintf("%s %s, 95%% CrI [%s, %s], %s, %s", fmt_num(r$est, 1), unit,
          fmt_num(r$lo, 1), fmt_num(r$hi, 1), pd_txt(r$pd), bf_txt(r))
}
BY_txt <- function(mod, a, b = "Control", par = "mu") {
  row_txt(BY_row(mod, a, b, par), if (par == "hu") "percentage points" else b_unit[[mod]])
}
GT_txt <- function(mod, grp, par = "mu") {
  row_txt(GT_row(mod, grp, par), if (par == "hu") "percentage points" else b_unit[[mod]])
}
# Within-group Polio - TB differences compare different sentences (or questions), so they
# are described (estimate and 95% CrI) but not tested; the interaction contrast is tested
GT_ci <- function(mod, grp, par = "mu") {
  r <- GT_row(mod, grp, par)
  sprintf("%s %s, 95%% CrI [%s, %s]", fmt_num(r$est, 1),
          if (par == "hu") "percentage points" else b_unit[[mod]], fmt_num(r$lo, 1), fmt_num(r$hi, 1))
}
# Evidence category of a Bayes factor [@leewagenmakers2014]
bf_strength <- function(bf) {
  b <- max(bf, 1 / bf)
  if (b > 100) "extreme" else if (b > 30) "very strong" else if (b > 10) "strong" else
    if (b > 3) "moderate" else "anecdotal"
}
B_ev <- \(...) bf_strength(BY_row(...)$BF10)
# Effect present: pd > 95% in the predicted (positive) direction; Bayes factors describe
# the strength of the evidence but are not a criterion
B_pos <- \(...) { r <- BY_row(...); r$est > 0 && r$pd > 0.95 }
B_bf10 <- \(...) BY_row(...)$BF10

# Model-estimated means: by status (pooled) or by condition within a topic
B_mean <- function(mod, lvl, par = "mu", tp = NULL, d = 1) {   # tp: by group (lvl) within topic tp
  m <- if (is.null(tp)) filter(bayes$means, status == lvl)
       else filter(bayes$means_topic, condition == lvl, topic == tp)
  m <- filter(m, model == mod, parameter == par)
  stopifnot(nrow(m) == 1)
  v <- b_scale[[mod]] * m$Mean
  if (b_scale[[mod]] == 100) paste0(fmt_num(v, d), "%") else paste(fmt_num(v, d), "ms per word")
}

# Prequestions: TB - Polio
PQB_mean <- \(cnd) {
  m <- filter(bayes$preq_means, condition == cnd)
  pct(m[[est_col(m)]])
}
# Described, not tested: each condition answered its own five questions, so the
# comparison is also one between two sets of questions
pq_row <- local({
  d <- bayes$preq_diff
  tibble(est = 100 * d[[est_col(d)]], lo = 100 * d$CI_low, hi = 100 * d$CI_high, pd = d$pd,
         lab = paste(d$Level1, "−", d$Level2))
})
PQB_diff <- sprintf("%s: %s percentage points, 95%% CrI [%s, %s], %s", pq_row$lab,
                    fmt_num(pq_row$est, 1), fmt_num(pq_row$lo, 1), fmt_num(pq_row$hi, 1),
                    pd_txt(pq_row$pd))

# TB group vs. no-prequestion group within a topic (descriptive, from the Group x Topic
# posterior draws): the comparison closest to Experiment 2 of Lewis & Mensink (2012), who
# used the same text with TB prequestions and a no-prequestion control
tb_row <- function(mod, tp, par = "mu") {
  d <- filter(bayes$means_topic_draws, model == mod, parameter == par, topic == tp,
              condition %in% c("TB", "Control")) |>
    select(draw, condition, value) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = condition, values_from = value) |>
    mutate(diff = b_scale[[mod]] * (TB - Control))
  tibble(est = mean(d$diff), lo = quantile(d$diff, 0.025), hi = quantile(d$diff, 0.975),
         pd = max(mean(d$diff > 0), mean(d$diff < 0)))
}
tb_txt <- function(mod, tp, par = "mu") {
  r <- tb_row(mod, tp, par)
  mn <- \(x) sub("^-", "−", fmt_num(x, 1))   # typographic minus
  sprintf("%s %s, 95%% CrI [%s, %s]", mn(r$est), b_unit[[mod]], mn(r$lo), mn(r$hi))
}

# Sampling diagnostics
diag_ok <- sum(bayes$diag$divergences) == 0 && max(bayes$diag$max_rhat) < 1.01

# Posterior figures: draws of the model-estimated means, pooled (by status) and within
# each topic (by condition, coloured by the status of the cell)
status_cols <- c(Prequestioned = "#E69F00", `Non-prequestioned` = "#56B4E9",
                 Control = "#999999")
post_plot <- function(keys, labels, unit_word) {
  topic_lab <- c(Polio = "Polio", TB = "TB")
  stat_lab <- c(Prequestioned = "Preq.", `Non-prequestioned` = "Non-preq.", Control = "No-preq.")
  cols <- c("Both topics (pooled)", "Polio group", "TB group", "No-prequestion group")
  d <- bind_rows(
    bayes$means_draws |>
      mutate(col = cols[1], x = stat_lab[as.character(status)]),
    bayes$means_topic_draws |>
      mutate(col = if_else(condition == "Control", "No-prequestion group", paste(condition, "group")),
             x = topic_lab[as.character(topic)])) |>
    # one key per plotted quantity: <model>_mu / <model>_tau for the ex-Gaussian models,
    # otherwise the model's main quantity ("mu")
    mutate(key = if_else(model %in% c("total_fix", "first_pass") | parameter != "mu",
                         paste(model, parameter, sep = "_"), model)) |>
    filter(key %in% keys) |>
    mutate(value = b_scale[model] * value,
           row = factor(labels[key], levels = labels[keys]),
           col = factor(col, levels = cols),
           x = factor(x, levels = c(stat_lab, topic_lab)),
           status = factor(status, levels = names(status_cols)))
  ggplot(d, aes(x, value, fill = status)) +
    ggdist::stat_halfeye(.width = c(0.66, 0.95), point_interval = "mean_qi",
                         slab_alpha = 0.85, point_size = 1.4, interval_size_range = c(0.5, 1.2)) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = status_cols, name = "Status of the material for the reader",
                      labels = c(Prequestioned = "Prequestioned", `Non-prequestioned` = "Non-prequestioned",
                                 Control = "No-prequestion")) +
    facet_grid(row ~ col, scales = "free", space = "free_x", switch = "y") +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
    theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), strip.placement = "outside",
          strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"), panel.spacing.x = unit(1.2, "lines"),
          axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7.5, lineheight = 0.9))
}
```

A common study strategy involves retrieving information from memory by answering questions after a learning event [@hartwig2012]. This technique, known as *retrieval practice*, has been shown to improve long-term retention across a wide range of materials and learning contexts, a phenomenon known as the *testing effect* [@carpenter2012; @dunlosky2013; @kornell2016; @roediger2006; @rowland2014]. Surprisingly, answering questions *before* a learning event can also improve subsequent memory, even when learners have little prior knowledge of the material and most of their initial answers are incorrect. This phenomenon, known as the *prequestion effect*, is particularly intriguing because, unlike traditional retrieval practice, it does not require learners to retrieve previously studied information. Although this finding is consistent with the broader literature suggesting that effortful and even error-prone learning experiences can benefit long-term retention [@bjork1994], why prequestions improve learning remains unclear.

The benefits of prequestions are typically demonstrated in experiments in which learners are assigned to a prequestion group or a control group [@carpenter2023]. Before encountering the learning material, the prequestion group attempts to answer questions about the upcoming content, often guessing when they do not know the answers, whereas the control group encounters the material without answering any questions. After learning, both groups complete a final memory test assessing information that was targeted by the prequestions as well as information that was not. The typical finding is that learners who received prequestions remember the targeted information better than those who did not, a phenomenon known as the specific benefit of prequestions [@pan2023]. In some cases, prequestions also improve memory for information that was not directly targeted, known as a general benefit of prequestions. However, whereas the specific benefit is robust, the general benefit is less consistent. Two recent meta-analyses found substantial specific benefits [g = 0.54, @sthilaire2023; g = 0.66, @kingshepard2025], but no reliable general benefit [g = 0.04, @sthilaire2023; g = 0.01, @kingshepard2025]. Nevertheless, some studies have reported general benefits depending on the learning materials [@carpenter2017], the types of questions used [@bostan2026; @sthilaire2019], and the placement of non-prequestioned information relative to prequestioned content [@sana2023]. The specific benefit, by contrast, has been demonstrated acorss a wide variety of study materials and settings [@richland2009; @carpenter2017; @sthilaire2020; @carpenter2018; @geller2017; @soderstrom2023; see @pan2023 for a review].

Why do preqeustions improve learning? Several non-mutually exclusive mechanisms have been proposed [@kingshepard2025; @pan2023]. Prequestions may stimulate curiosity about the answers [@berlyne1954; @berlyne1962], encourage elaboration by activating related prior knowledge [@kornell2009], or provide a metacognitive "reality check" that makes learners aware of gaps in their knowledge [@bjork2013]. Although these explanations differ, they share the possibility that prequestions direct learners' attention toward information relevant to the questions [@kingshepard2025]. According to an *attention-based account*, prequestions signal which information is important, encouraging learners to attend to and process that information more thoroughly when they encounter it [@pan2023]. Consistent with this account, researchers looking at eye movements during a learning episode have found that learners spend more time looking at [@bostan2026; @yang2021], re-inspecting, and returning to prequestioned information after reading subsequent material [@lewis2012].

Although these findings support an attention-based account, several results suggest that directing attention toward prequestioned information may not, by itself, fully explain the benefits of prequestions. If prequestions primarily function by signaling which information deserves attention, other methods of highlighting that information might be expected to produce similar benefits. However, answering prequestions has been found to improve memory more than studying material with the tested concepts emphasized or reading questions without answering them [@richland2009], and more than reading learning objectives or statements of the target facts [@sana2020; but see @rivers2026]. Moreover, although prequestions reliably improve memory for targeted information [@kingshepard2025; @sthilaire2023], some studies also find benefits for information that was not prequestioned [@bostan2026; @rivers2026; @sana2023; @sthilaire2019]. Any account of the prequestion effect must therefore consider why learning benefits are sometimes restricted to prequestioned information and sometimes extend to other material.

One account that may be able to explain these differences is the *attentional-window account* [@sana2023]. According to this account, prequestions initiate a period of heightened attention as learners search for the answers, with attention returning to baseline once the relevant information has been encountered. Information presented while this attentional window remains open may also benefit, even if it was not directly targeted by a prequestion. Thus, whether prequestions produce a general benefit should depend partly on where the prequestioned information appears in the learning material. Supporting this prediction, @sana2023 found that prequestions produced only a specific benefit when the targeted information appeared near the beginning of a passage. However, when the targeted information appeared near the end, prequestions also improved memory for non-prequestioned information encountered while learners were presumably still searching for the answers. These findings suggest that the effects of prequestions may depend on how attention is allocated throughout the learning event. Nevertheless, much of the evidence for this account comes from subsequent memory performance rather than direct observations of processing during learning.

Eye tracking provides a way to examine these attentional predictions as learning unfolds. During reading and visual exploration, the eyes alternate between relatively brief periods of stability, known as fixations, and rapid movements between them, known as saccades. The location and duration of fixations provide measures of overt visual attention and are sensitive to cognitive processes involved in comprehension and learning [@deng2023; @hyona2003; @madsen2021; @rayner1998; @rayner2009]. Because eye movements can be recorded continuously without interrupting the learning experience, eye tracking allows researchers to examine how learners visually process information as they encounter it rather than inferring processing solely from subsequent memory performance [@rayner1998]. Importantly, eye movements can distinguish processing during an initial encounter with information from subsequent reprocessing, such as rereading a sentence or returning to an earlier part of a passage. Eye-movement measures are also sensitive to individual differences in reading ability [@ashby2005; @perfetti2007], prior knowledge [@mcnamara2009], and working memory capacity [@daneman1980]. Accordingly, real-time measures such as eye tracking have been identified as an important direction for prequestion research [@pan2023]. In particular, @kingshepard2025 recommended examining how prequestions influence the time learners spend processing prequestioned and non-prequestioned information during reading.

Relatively few studies have used eye tracking to investigate how prequestions influence reading. In an early study, readers who received questions before reading spent more time rereading and carefully processing question-related information while reading unrelated material more quickly [@rothkopf1979]. @lewis2012 examined the effects of prequestions in two eye-tracking experiments using passages on different topics. In Experiment 1, participants read a passage about space travel after receiving one of two sets of six prequestions or no prequestions. Readers receiving one set of prequestions spent more time re-inspecting and looking back to question-relevant sentences and subsequently recalled more of that information than readers receiving the other set. However, the second set of prequestions did not produce reliable effects on reading or memory. In Experiment 2, @lewis2012 used a passage describing the humanitarian efforts of the Gates Foundation, including efforts to address polio and tuberculosis (TB). One group received four prequestions about TB before reading, whereas a control group read the passage without prequestions. Eye movements were recorded using a head-mounted eye tracker. Prequestions did not increase forward reading times for sentences containing the answers. Instead, readers who received prequestions spent more time rereading the targeted sentences before moving forward and made more look-backs to those sentences after proceeding to later portions of the passage. They also showed a smaller increase in look-backs to other parts of the text. On a subsequent free-recall test, the prequestion group recalled approximately twice as much of the targeted information as the control group, but did not recall more of the non-prequestioned information. Thus, the specific memory benefit was accompanied by greater reprocessing of the targeted sentences rather than slower initial reading. This pattern suggests that readers may first recognize information as relevant to a prequestion and subsequently return to process it more extensively.

More recently, @bostan2026 examined the effects of *integrative prequestions*, which require learners to combine information from different parts of a text. Twelve participants received integrative prequestions before reading a passage about car brakes, whereas another twelve read the passage without prequestions. Compared with the control group, readers who received prequestions made more fixations, spent more time on targeted sentences, and made more transitions between them. Unlike most prequestion studies, the authors also observed a general benefit: participants who received prequestions performed better on questions assessing non-prequestioned information despite spending less time fixating those sentences. These findings suggest that prequestions can alter the distribution of visual processing across a passage, although increased fixation time on particular information does not necessarily correspond to greater memory for that information.

Taken together, previous eye-tracking studies indicate that prequestions influence how learners allocate visual attention during reading [@bostan2026; @lewis2012; @yang2021]. However, whether these changes contribute directly to improved memory or reflect other processes initiated by prequestions remains uncertain. Furthermore, some findings suggest that the benefits of prequestions cannot be explained simply by the amount of time learners spend processing the material. For example, in a large multisite classroom study, prequestions improved learning even though students subsequently watched less of the instructional videos, with some students skipping the videos entirely [@motz2026]. Similarly, @bostan2026 found improved memory for non-prequestioned information despite shorter fixation times on that information. Such findings suggest that prequestions may influence not only the allocation of attention but also how information is processed once encountered.

One alternative explanation is the *mental model hypothesis* proposed by @motz2026. According to this account, prequestions activate relevant prior knowledge before learning, facilitating the processing and encoding of related information when it is subsequently encountered. As learners recognize connections between the new information and their activated knowledge, they may allocate additional attention to that content. From this perspective, increased attention may follow the recognition of relevant information rather than being the primary mechanism responsible for improved learning. Consistent with this possibility, @motz2026 found that the benefit of prequestions was greater among students who answered more prequestions correctly, suggesting that access to relevant prior knowledge may contribute to the effect. Although the attention-based and mental model accounts are not necessarily mutually exclusive, they raise an important question about the timing and nature of the processing changes associated with prequestions. In particular, determining whether prequestions influence reading when relevant information is first encountered or primarily during subsequent reprocessing may help clarify how prequestions shape learning.

## The Current Study

The existing literature provides evidence that prequestions influence both memory and the allocation of visual attention during learning. However, questions remain about when these changes in visual processing emerge, whether they are specific to prequestioned information, and how prequestions alter the distribution of reading times. The current study addressed these questions by combining a counterbalanced prequestion design with eye-tracking measures that distinguish initial reading from subsequent reprocessing. We also used distributional analyses to examine how prequestions influence reading times beyond differences in average duration.

Our study builds on two previous eye-tracking investigations of prequestions during reading [@lewis2012; @bostan2026] while addressing several methodological limitations. First, in Experiment 2 of @lewis2012 and in @bostan2026, the same set of sentences was prequestioned for all participants in the prequestion condition. Consequently, the effects of prequestions could not be fully separated from characteristics of the particular sentences being targeted. Although Experiment 1 of @lewis2012 included two sets of prequestions, these targeted different numbers of sentences, and only one set reliably affected reading. In the current study, prequestioned content was fully counterbalanced so that the same sentences were read both with and without prequestions across participants.

Second, previous studies used relatively small samples, with approximately 20 participants per group in @lewis2012 and 12 participants per group in @bostan2026, limiting the precision of the estimated effects. In addition, @bostan2026 compared total fixation durations and counts between groups without accounting for participant-level differences in reading behavior. The current study included a substantially larger sample (`r n_total` participants, approximately `r round(mean(n_by_cond$n))` per condition) and used models that accounted for variation across participants and items, including sentences and test questions where appropriate. Third, whereas previous studies primarily analyzed average reading or fixation times, we also examined the distribution of reading times to determine whether prequestions produce broader shifts in reading duration or disproportionately influence unusually long readings.

Fourth, in @lewis2012, participants were presented with questions and instructed to read the passage to answer them, but were not required to provide answers before reading. Although learners may have generated answers covertly, which can be as effective as overtly answering prequestions [@rivers2026], whether they did so is unknown. In the current study, participants explicitly answered each prequestion before reading, consistent with the procedure used in many prequestion studies. Finally, unlike the integrative questions used by @bostan2026, each prequestion in the current study targeted information contained within a single sentence, as in @lewis2012. Such questions have generally been associated with specific rather than general memory benefits [@sthilaire2019].

In out study, participants read the Gates Foundation passage used in Experiment 2 of @lewis2012, which describes efforts to eradicate polio and TB. Before reading, participants answered five prequestions about polio, five prequestions about TB, or no prequestions. The passage contained ten target sentences, each providing the answer to one prequestion. By counterbalancing which topic was prequestioned, every target sentence served as prequestioned information for one group and non-prequestioned information for another. This design allowed us to compare processing of the same sentences across prequestion and no-prequestion conditions while minimizing confounding between prequestion status and sentence content.

We examined two categories of eye-movement measures. *Global measures*, including total gaze duration, rereading time, and regressions-in (look-backs), captured processing across encounters with a sentence, including subsequent returns to it. Our *local measure*, selective regression-path duration, captured processing associated with the initial encounter with a sentence, before the reader progressed to later text. Distinguishing these measures allowed us to assess whether prequestions influence processing when relevant information is first encountered, during subsequent rereading, or both.

In addition to examining these measures, we used distributional analyses to characterize how prequestions influence reading times. Reading and fixation durations are typically right-skewed, with a lower bound of zero and a relatively long tail of unusually long observations [@balota2011; @staub2010]. Consequently, statistical models that assume normally distributed reading times may not adequately characterize the observed data, and transformations intended to reduce skewness can alter the scale on which effects are evaluated [@lo2015]. We therefore modeled total gaze duration using the ex-Gaussian distribution, which represents response times as the sum of a Gaussian component, characterized by its mean (μ), and an exponential component, characterized by its mean (τ).

An advantage of the ex-Gaussian distribution is that it allows changes in the location of the Gaussian component to be distinguished from changes in the exponential component contributing to the right tail. Although these parameters are descriptive and do not uniquely identify underlying cognitive processes [@matzke2009], previous research suggests that experimental manipulations can influence them differently. For example, word frequency has been found to affect both μ and τ in fixation durations during reading [@staub2010], whereas modest visual degradation of text primarily affected μ [@white2012]. Similarly, in scene viewing, image type influenced μ, whereas familiarity increased τ, reflecting a greater contribution from longer fixations [@guy2020]. These findings illustrate how experimental manipulations may alter different characteristics of the reading-time distribution.

This distinction may be particularly informative for understanding prequestion effects. If prequestions lead readers to recognize particular sentences as relevant and sometimes engage in additional processing or reanalysis, they may disproportionately increase longer reading times rather than uniformly slowing reading. Analyses of average reading duration alone cannot distinguish these possibilities. We therefore examined both ex-Gaussian parameters. An effect on μ would indicate a shift in the Gaussian component of the reading-time distribution, whereas an effect on τ would indicate a greater contribution from the exponential component and its right tail. Although neither pattern provides a unique signature of a cognitive mechanism, these analyses allow a more detailed characterization of how prequestions change reading behavior.

### Hypotheses

For final test performance, we predicted a *specific benefit* of prequestions: participants would remember more information about the prequestioned topic than participants in the no-prequestion condition. Based on prior findings that general benefits are less consistent, particularly for questions targeting individual pieces of information [@sthilaire2019; @kingshepard2025], we did not predict a general benefit for the non-prequestioned topic. We compared performance for prequestioned and non-prequestioned information against performance for the same material in the no-prequestion condition, both overall and separately for each topic.

For eye movements, we predicted that prequestioned sentences would receive longer total gaze durations and more rereading than the same sentences encountered without prequestions. Specifically, we expected an interaction between prequestion condition and topic, such that Polio prequestions would selectively increase processing of polio-related sentences, whereas TB prequestions would selectively increase processing of TB-related sentences. We also examined whether these changes emerged during initial reading or subsequent reprocessing. Finally, our distributional analyses assessed whether differences in total gaze duration were associated with changes in the Gaussian component (μ), the exponential component (τ), or both.

# Method

We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions, all manipulations, and all measures included in the study. The study was preregistered (`r if (masked) 'https://osf.io/8env4/overview?view_only=5073f3b1114944c1a6c63339132a5ad5' else 'https://osf.io/8env4'`). All data, materials, and analysis scripts are available at `r if (masked) 'https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Prequestions_EyeTracking-B118/' else 'https://github.com/jgeller112/Prequestions_EyeTracking'`. All reported statistics, tables, and figures were generated from the raw data using the code in that repository. Generative AI (Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic) was used to assist with editing the manuscript and code as well as help organzie all the data and code on the repository. The author verified the content and citations and takes full responsibility for the manuscript.

## Participants

The target sample size was determined based on the specific benefit of prequestions. A recent meta-analysis reported a medium-sized effect (*g* = 0.54; @sthilaire2023), which we converted to an odds ratio of 2.66 for the preregistered binomial mixed-effects model. A simulation-based power analysis using mixedpower [@kumle2021], informed by pilot data, indicated that 45 participants per condition would provide 90% power to detect an effect of this magnitude. We therefore planned to recruit 135 participants, with 45 assigned to each of the three conditions.

Participants were recruited from the `r if (masked) 'university' else 'Boston College'` SONA participant pool and received course credit. Eye-tracking data were recorded from `r n_recordings` participants. `r excl_n(excluded_incomplete, "had eye-tracking data for fewer than all four pages of the text")` `r excl_n(excluded_calibration, "did not meet the preregistered calibration criterion (accuracy and precision of 0.5° or better) or could not be calibrated")` `r excl_n(excluded_no_pretest, "were in a prequestion condition but had no prequestion responses")` `r excl_n(excluded_no_test, "had no final test data")` The final sample comprised `r n_total` participants (no prequestions: `r n_by_cond$n[1]`; Polio prequestions: `r n_by_cond$n[2]`; TB prequestions: `r n_by_cond$n[3]`).

`r if (calib_n == n_total) 'Calibration validation data were available for all included participants.' else sprintf('Calibration validation data were available for %d of the %d included participants.', calib_n, n_total)` Mean calibration accuracy was `r num(calib_summary$accuracy_M, 2)`° (*SD* = `r num(calib_summary$accuracy_SD, 2)`, range `r num(calib_summary$accuracy_min, 2)`–`r num(calib_summary$accuracy_max, 2)`), and mean precision, defined as the standard deviation of gaze samples, was `r num(calib_summary$precision_M, 2)`° (*SD* = `r num(calib_summary$precision_SD, 2)`, range `r num(calib_summary$precision_min, 2)`–`r num(calib_summary$precision_max, 2)`). All included participants with available calibration data met the preregistered criterion of 0.5° or better for both accuracy and precision. The preregistered exclusion criterion for high prior knowledge was not applied.

## Materials

Participants read a `r num(n_words_passage)`-word passage used by @lewis2012 describing the Gates Foundation's humanitarian efforts to eradicate polio and tuberculosis (TB) in developing countries. The passage contained `r n_sentences` sentences presented across four pages, each consisting of 16–17 lines (@fig-aois). Ten sentences served as targets: five concerning polio (`r WT("PO")`) and five concerning TB (`r WT("TB")`).

The polio target sentences had a higher reading level than the TB target sentences, as assessed by the Flesch–Kincaid grade level [@kincaid1975], calculated using the quanteda package [@quanteda2018] (polio: `r TM("PO", "fk")`; TB: `r TM("TB", "fk")`). However, the two sets of sentences were similar in syntactic complexity, estimated using dependency parsing with UDPipe [@straka2017; @R-udpipe] and its English Web Treebank model [@silveira2014]. We examined mean dependency distance [@liu2008], defined as the average number of words separating a word from its syntactic head (polio: `r TM("PO", "mdd", 2)`; TB: `r TM("TB", "mdd", 2)`), and the number of clauses per sentence (polio: `r TM("PO", "clauses")`; TB: `r TM("TB", "clauses")`).

Each target sentence contained the answer to one of ten short-answer questions (five about polio and five about TB; @apx-a). Questions required percentage-based, yes/no, or multipart responses. The maximum possible score was `r points_by_topic$points[1]` points per topic and `r sum(points_by_topic$points)` points overall.

The study included three conditions: polio prequestions, TB prequestions, and no prequestions. Participants in the polio and TB conditions answered five questions about their assigned topic before reading, whereas participants in the no-prequestion condition read the passage without answering questions beforehand. For each prequestion condition, the five target sentences corresponding to the assigned topic were classified as *prequestioned*, and the five sentences about the other topic were classified as *non-prequestioned*. Thus, across conditions, every target sentence served as both prequestioned and non-prequestioned information, allowing the effects of prequestions to be separated from differences in sentence content.

## Apparatus

Eye movements were recorded using a Tobii Pro Spectrum eye tracker sampling at 600 Hz. The passage was displayed on a 23.8-inch EIZO FlexScan EV2451 monitor (1920 × 1080 pixels) viewed from approximately 65 cm without a chin rest. Text was presented in 36-point Courier New, a monospaced font, against a grey background. At this viewing distance, each character subtended approximately 0.5° of visual angle, and the line spacing subtended approximately 1.1°.

The experiment was administered using Tobii Pro Lab (version 25.19). The prequestions, distractor task, and final test were programmed in PsychoPy, hosted on Pavlovia, and embedded as web elements within the Tobii Pro Lab timeline.

## Procedure

At the beginning of the session, participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: polio prequestions, TB prequestions, or no prequestions. The experiment consisted of four phases: prequestions, reading, a distractor task, and a final test. Participants in the no-prequestion condition skipped the prequestion phase.

### Prequestions

Participants in the two prequestion conditions answered five short-answer questions about their assigned topic (polio or TB), presented in random order (`r msk('https://run.pavlovia.org/Jgeller112/preq')`). They were informed that they might not know the correct answers and were encouraged to provide their best guesses. Each question appeared individually on the screen, with a text box below it for entering a response. Participants had unlimited time to respond and clicked a triangle at the bottom of the screen to advance to the next question. No feedback was provided.

### Reading

Before reading, participants completed Tobii Pro Lab's nine-point calibration procedure, which presented white targets against a grey background. Calibration accuracy and precision were then validated and recorded. Participants subsequently read the four-page passage while their eye movements were recorded. They advanced through the pages at their own pace, with no time limit, but could not return to previously viewed pages.

### Distractor Task

After reading, all participants completed a president recognition task (`r msk('https://run.pavlovia.org/Jgeller112/preq_president')`) that served as a distractor and lasted approximately 3 minutes.

### Final Test

Participants completed a final test consisting of all ten short-answer questions (five about polio and five about TB), presented in random order (`r msk('https://run.pavlovia.org/Jgeller112/preQ_test')`). The response format was identical to that used during the prequestion phase, with unlimited response time and no feedback. For participants in the prequestion conditions, five questions were repeated from the prequestion phase, whereas the remaining five were new. Participants were then thanked and debriefed.

## Scoring

Prequestion and final-test responses were scored using a deterministic, rule-based scoring procedure developed with the assistance of Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic; model ID `claude-opus-5-5`). Rather than scoring individual responses directly, Claude generated an R scoring script (`scoring_rubric.R`, used by `grade_prequestions.R` and `grade_test.R`) that applied the same predefined criteria to all responses. The script awarded one point for each required element of a correct answer present in a participant's response. Question-specific scoring criteria are provided in @apx-a.

To assess scoring reliability, a research assistant who was blind to experimental condition, test phase, and automated scores independently scored all `r format(rater$overall$n, big.mark = ',')` nonblank responses. The automated and human scores agreed exactly on `r pct(rater$overall$exact)` of responses. Agreement was excellent, ICC(2,1) = `r sub('^0', '', fmt_num(rater$overall$icc, 2))`, 95% CI [`r sub('^0', '', fmt_num(rater$overall$icc_lo, 2))`, `r sub('^0', '', fmt_num(rater$overall$icc_hi, 2))`], based on a two-way random-effects, absolute-agreement, single-measure intraclass correlation coefficient [@shrout1979; @koo2016], calculated using the irr package [@R-irr]. Agreement for participants' total final-test scores was also excellent, ICC(2,1) = `r sub('^0', '', fmt_num(rater$totals$icc, 2))`. Question-level agreement statistics are reported in @tbl-scoring. All analyses used the automated scores.

## Eye-Movement Data Processing

```{r}
#| label: drift-example
#| include: false
# Example reader (drift_id, fx_drift) and drift statistics (drift_stats, drift_ex):
# data/derived/manuscript_inputs.rds
drift_panel <- function(yvar, svar, title) {
  ggplot(fx_drift, aes(x, 1 - .data[[yvar]])) +
    annotation_raster(img2, 0, 1, 0, 1) +
    geom_rect(data = targets2, inherit.aes = FALSE,
              aes(xmin = x0, xmax = x1, ymin = 1 - y1, ymax = 1 - y0),
              fill = NA, colour = "grey20", linewidth = 0.3, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_path(colour = "grey35", alpha = 0.45, linewidth = 0.25) +
    geom_point(aes(size = duration, colour = factor(.data[[svar]], levels = 1:11),
                   shape = reading), stroke = 0.6, alpha = 0.85) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 16, `FALSE` = 1), guide = "none") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = sentence_cols,
                        na.value = "grey55", name = "Sentence", drop = FALSE) +
    scale_size_area(max_size = 2.6, name = "Duration (ms)") +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), expand = c(0, 0)) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), expand = c(0, 0)) +
    coord_fixed(9 / 16) +
    labs(title = title) +
    theme_void(base_size = 9) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 9, face = "bold"))
}
```

Sentence-level measures were computed from the fixation-level data. Fixations were identified with Tobii Pro Lab's Tobii I-VT (Fixation) filter, a velocity-threshold identification algorithm [@salvucci2000; @olsen2012], with the following settings. Gaps in the gaze data shorter than 75 ms (e.g., brief losses of tracking) were filled by linear interpolation, the gaze positions of the two eyes were averaged, and noise was reduced with a moving median over a window of three samples. A gaze sample was classified as part of a fixation when the angular velocity of the eye, computed over a 20-ms window, was below 30°/s. Adjacent fixations separated by less than 75 ms and less than 0.5° of visual angle were merged, and fixations shorter than 60 ms were discarded. Fixations cut off when a page appeared or disappeared can nonetheless be shorter than 60 ms in the export. We excluded fixations shorter than 80 ms (`r pct(share_short)` of fixations) and longer than 1,000 ms (`r pct(share_long, 2)`) before any further processing. Both bounds follow common practice in reading research: 80 ms is the most common lower bound, and 800, 1,000, and 1,200 ms are the most common upper bounds [@schotter2025; e.g., @serranocarot2025]. Very short fixations are unlikely to reflect processing of the text and include fixations cut short by a page change. Most fixations in reading last around 200 ms [@schotter2025; @rayner1998]; in the present data the median fixation lasted `r round(fix_median)` ms, so a single fixation longer than 1,000 ms, `r fmt_num(1000 / fix_median, 1)` times the median, is unlikely to reflect ongoing reading and more likely reflects a lapse of attention or a brief loss of the eye-tracking signal that the fixation filter bridged.

The remaining processing (`derive_et_measures.R`) proceeded in four steps. (a) The exact layout of each page was reconstructed from the sentence texts and full-resolution screenshots of the pages (monospaced font, 79 characters per line), giving the screen position of every character of every sentence (@fig-aois). (b) Each fixation was assigned to a text line after correcting for vertical drift, separately for each reader and page, with a procedure that combines two approaches used in automated drift-correction algorithms [@carr2022]: assigning sequences of fixations to a line together, and modelling drift as a function of position on the page (details in @apx-d). The correction was limited to the calibration accuracy criterion of 0.5° (`r num(max_shift_cm, 2)` cm, about 0.45 of a line spacing), so it could not move a reader's gaze by a whole line. (c) Each fixation was then assigned to the sentence occupying its line and horizontal position: its character column was computed from the fixed character width, a fixation on a space took the sentence of the nearest letter, and fixations more than three characters beyond either end of a line were treated as off the text. (d) Reading on each page was taken to start at the first fixation on the page's first sentence; fixations before that (the landing) contributed to total time but not to first-pass measures. After processing, `r pct(share_assigned)` of on-screen fixations were assigned to a sentence, and the assigned sentence agreed with Tobii Pro Lab's assignment for `r pct(share_agree)` of fixations. First-pass reading was identified for `r pct(fp_present_derived)` of fixated target sentences. @fig-scanpath shows one reader's fixations on one page before and after processing. For this reader, the correction moved fixations by a median of `r num(drift_ex$shift, 2)` line spacings and changed the sentence assigned to `r pct(drift_ex$relabelled)` of fixations; the medians over all readers and pages were `r num(median(drift_stats$shift), 2)` line spacings and `r pct(median(drift_stats$relabelled))`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-aois
#| fig-cap: "The Four Text Pages and the Sentence Regions Used as Areas of Interest"
#| apa-note: "Each sentence is one area of interest, made of one rectangle per text line it occupies. Polio target sentences are shown in blue, TB target sentences in vermillion (orange-red), and other sentences in grey; numbers give each sentence's position on its page. Page 4 contains no target sentences."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
wrap_plots(map(1:4, \(p) page_panel(p, label_size = 3.4)), ncol = 2, guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-scanpath
#| fig-cap: "One Reader's Fixations on One Page Before and After Processing"
#| apa-note: "One participant in the TB prequestion condition, page 2, chosen to illustrate vertical drift. (A) Recorded gaze positions, coloured by the sentence assigned by Tobii Pro Lab. (B) The same fixations after drift correction (single vertical offset, assignment of chains of fixations to lines, and a linear drift model, limited to 0.5°; see Appendix D), coloured by the sentence assigned in processing. Each point is one fixation (size proportional to duration); grey points were not assigned to any sentence. Lines join consecutive fixations. Open circles are fixations made before reading started on the page. Dashed rectangles outline the target sentences."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 7.2
(drift_panel("y_recorded", "sentence_tobii",
             "A. Before correction: recorded gaze, Tobii Pro Lab sentence labels") /
   drift_panel("y_corrected", "sentence_corrected",
               "B. After correction: drift-corrected gaze and sentence labels")) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "right", legend.key.size = unit(0.35, "cm"))
```

## Eye-Movement Measures

All measures were computed for each participant and target sentence. Durations were divided by the number of words in the sentence (ms per word), because target sentences differed in length. Only sentences that were fixated were analysed: a target sentence that received no fixation has no reading time, so its measures were treated as missing (`r n_not_fixated` of `r n_dat` target sentences, `r pct(n_not_fixated / n_dat)`). Following the eye-movement literature, we distinguish *global* measures, which reflect all processing of a sentence including later returns to it, from *local* measures, which reflect processing when the sentence is first encountered (@fig-measures).

```{r}
#| label: fig-measures
#| fig-cap: "Eye-Movement Measures, Illustrated With a Schematic Reading Example"
#| apa-note: "Definitions follow @schotter2025. The circles are fixations, numbered in time order (arrows: saccades; dashed arrows: regressions; dotted arrows: moves to the next line); the shaded sentence is the target, and each fixation is coloured by the measure it counts towards for the target. *Selective regression-path duration* (first-pass reading; also called right-bounded reading time or selective go-past time) sums the fixations on the sentence from first entering it until the eyes first move past it to later text; fixations on earlier text during this period (here, 6) are not counted and do not end it. *Total gaze duration* sums all fixations on the sentence. *Regression-in* records whether the eyes returned to the sentence from later text (0/1). *Re-reading time* sums the fixations on the sentence after the reader had first moved on to later text (operationalizing the preregistered \"re-reading durations back to the prequestioned information\"). Selective regression-path duration is defined only for sentences fixated before any later sentence (not skipped). The duration measures do not overlap: total gaze duration is the sum of selective regression-path duration, re-reading time, and any fixations made before reading started on the page. Global measures include later returns to the sentence; the local measure reflects processing when the sentence is first encountered. The preregistered first-pass duration (fixations until the sentence is first exited) would here be 3 + 4 + 5 only, cut short by the brief return at 6; it was replaced by selective regression-path duration (see Statistical Analysis). All durations were divided by the number of words in the sentence (ms per word)."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.1
measures_schematic()
```

## Statistical Analysis

All analyses were conducted in R version `r paste(R.version$major, R.version$minor, sep = '.')` [@R-base].^[`r software_footnote`] The effects of prequestions on test performance and eye movements were estimated with Bayesian mixed models in brms [@brms2017], which fits models in Stan [@stan2017], run through cmdstanr [@R-cmdstanr] with CmdStan `r as.character(cmdstanr::cmdstan_version())`. Each target sentence, and each final-test question, was coded by its status for the reader: *prequestioned* (Polio sentences and questions for readers in the Polio condition, TB sentences and questions for readers in the TB condition), *non-prequestioned* (the other topic for those readers), or *no-prequestion* (both topics for readers in the no-prequestion condition). The main models pooled the two prequestion conditions, with Status and Topic (Polio, TB) as fixed effects. The *specific effect* of prequestions was the difference prequestioned − no-prequestion: the same sentences or questions for readers whose prequestions they answered and for readers who saw no prequestions. The *general effect* was non-prequestioned − no-prequestion. Because each topic contributes equally to the prequestioned, non-prequestioned, and no-prequestion cells, differences between the Polio and TB materials cancel in these comparisons. Both the specific and general effects and their breakdown by topic were preregistered. To break the effects down by topic, we fitted the preregistered Group (Polio prequestions, TB prequestions, or no prequestions) × Topic (Polio, TB) models with the same families and priors. Following the preregistered hypotheses, we estimated the Polio − TB difference within each group—predicted to be positive in the Polio group, negative in the TB group, and absent in the no-prequestion group—and the Group × Topic interaction contrast, the Polio group's Polio − TB difference minus the TB group's, predicted to be positive. Because the Polio and TB sentences (and questions) are different items, each within-group Polio − TB difference combines any effect of prequestions with differences between the items, and with five items per topic, the population-level topic difference is estimated imprecisely. Each within-group difference was therefore interpreted together with the interaction contrast, in which the item differences cancel because both groups read the same items.

Reading times are strongly right-skewed, so no duration was analysed with a Gaussian model. As preregistered for heavily skewed durations, total gaze duration was analysed with an ex-Gaussian distributional model ({cogmod}; @R-cogmod), which describes a duration as the sum of a Gaussian component, whose mean μ reflects typical reading time, and an exponential component, whose mean τ reflects the tail of unusually long readings. The mean of an ex-Gaussian distribution is μ + τ and its standard deviation is √(σ² + τ²), where σ is the standard deviation of the Gaussian component, so μ and τ are components of reading time rather than reading times themselves. The fixed and random effects applied to both μ and τ, and σ had by-participant random intercepts. The preregistered first-pass duration, from first entering a sentence until first leaving it, could not be described by any of the distributions we considered (ex-Gaussian, Gamma, lognormal), because it mixes two kinds of first pass. About half of first passes, in all three conditions, were cut short after a few fixations by a brief return to the preceding line, so the distribution had two modes: interrupted first passes of a few hundred milliseconds and complete first readings of several seconds. First-pass reading was therefore measured as selective regression-path duration [also called right-bounded reading time; @schotter2025]: the time spent on the sentence from first entering it until the eyes first moved past it to later text, so that brief returns to earlier text did not end it and time spent on earlier text was not counted (@fig-measures). Its distribution was unimodal and right-skewed and closely described by the ex-Gaussian, so it was analysed with the same ex-Gaussian model as total gaze duration (μ and τ). Re-reading time was the time spent on a sentence after the reader had first moved on to later text, so that the two measures do not overlap [cf. rereading time in @schotter2025]. Whether readers returned to a sentence from later text is captured by regressions-in (0/1), which were analysed with logistic models; re-reading time was analysed for the `r pct(1 - share_not_reread)` of sentences that were re-read, with a Gamma model with a log link, which models positive, right-skewed durations without transforming them [@lo2015]; the ex-Gaussian was not suitable, because re-reading times were close to exponentially distributed, so that its Gaussian component collapsed (σ near zero). The model therefore describes how long readers re-read a sentence once they had returned to it. Because the questions were worth different numbers of points (1–4), final test performance was analysed as the points earned on each question out of its maximum, with a beta-binomial model: a binomial model of the points earned with an additional parameter for overdispersion, because a participant tends to know all or none of a question's elements. Effects are reported on the scale of the expected proportion of a question's points, which puts all questions on the same 0–1 scale. Because each question has at most four points, scores can take only a few values (0, .25, .33, .50, .67, .75, and 1). In posterior predictive checks, the beta-binomial model reproduced how often each score occurred (predicted and observed shares within `r fmt_num(100 * max(abs(filter(bayes$score_fit, model == 'Beta-binomial')$predicted - filter(bayes$score_fit, model == 'Beta-binomial')$observed)), 1)` percentage points), better than a binomial model without overdispersion. Prequestion performance was analysed in the same way, comparing the two prequestion conditions.

All models included the maximal random-effects structure warranted by the design [@barr2013]. Topic varied within participants, so the models included by-participant random intercepts and Topic slopes (the preregistered structure). Every target sentence and every final-test question was prequestioned for one group, non-prequestioned for another, and read or answered by the no-prequestion group, so Status (and Group) varied within items, and the models also included by-sentence (eye movements) or by-question (final test) random intercepts and Status (or Group) slopes. Within a participant, Status is determined by Topic, so no by-participant Status slope was possible. In the prequestion model, condition varied between participants and between questions, so it included random intercepts for participants and questions only. Status, Condition, and Topic were coded with equal-prior contrasts [`contr.equalprior_pairs`; {bayestestR}, @bayestestR2019]. With this coding, a normal(0, *s*) prior on the coefficients implies the same normal(0, *s*) prior on every pairwise difference between conditions, so that no condition serves as a reference with a different prior, and every comparison is tested against the same prior. *s* was set on each model's link scale: `r bayes$settings$s_logit` on the log-odds scale (regressions-in, final test, and prequestions; an odds ratio of `r fmt_num(exp(bayes$settings$s_logit), 1)` for one *SD*), `r bayes$settings$s_log` on the log scale of the Gamma models and on the scale of τ (a factor of about `r fmt_num(exp(bayes$settings$s_log), 2)` for one *SD*), and `r num(1000 * bayes$settings$s_mu)` ms per word for μ. Intercepts, random-effect standard deviations, and correlations had weakly informative priors (@apx-b). Each model was sampled with `r n_word(bayes$settings$chains)` chains of `r num(bayes$settings$iter - bayes$settings$warmup)` post-warm-up iterations (`r num(bayes$n_draws)` posterior draws, enough for stable Bayes factors). `r if (diag_ok) sprintf("All models converged: there were no divergent transitions, all R-hat values were below %s, and all bulk effective sample sizes exceeded %s.", fmt_num(max(bayes$diag$max_rhat) + 0.0005, 3), num(floor(min(bayes$diag$min_ess_bulk) / 100) * 100)) else stop("Revise: convergence sentence")`

Means and comparisons were computed on the response scale by averaging each posterior draw's predictions over the observed sample (modelbased with the {marginaleffects}[@marginaleffects2024] backend and `estimate = "average"`), so that they incorporate the variation due to the random effects. Durations are reported in ms per word, and probabilities and proportions in percent. Effects were summarized by their posterior mean, 95% credible interval (CrI), and probability of direction (pd), the proportion of the posterior with the same sign as its median. The pd is closely related to the frequentist *p* value: for a one-tailed test, *p* ≈ 1 − pd, and for a two-tailed test, *p* ≈ 2(1 − pd), so pd > 95% corresponds to a one-tailed *p* < .05 [@makowski2019]. The predictions for the specific effects and for prequestioned versus non-prequestioned material were directional (longer reading, more regressions, better recall), so we treated such an effect as present when pd > 95% in the predicted direction. The general effects had no directional prediction, so for them we required pd > 97.5%, corresponding to a two-tailed *p* < .05. Bayes factors were not used as a decision criterion; we report them to describe the strength of the evidence for or against each effect. Because pd only indicates the direction of an effect and cannot provide evidence that an effect is absent, we also computed Bayes factors. Each Bayes factor compares a model in which the comparison equals 0 with one in which it is free, using the Savage–Dickey density ratio [@wagenmakers2010]: the posterior density of the comparison at 0 divided by its prior density at 0. The prior densities came from the same models sampled from their priors only, and both densities were computed for the comparisons on the link scale, where the equal priors apply. For τ and for the expected re-reading time, which have no single link scale, they were computed on the response scale; for the expected re-reading time, at the population level (without random effects), because averaging over random effects drawn from their priors produced prior draws too extreme for a density estimate. For the Group × Topic comparisons of look-backs and final test scores, the Bayes factors were also computed on the response scale (probabilities and proportions of points), the scale of the estimates. These comparisons involve different Polio and TB items, some of which had outcomes near 0 or 1, and for such outcomes the same comparison is much less precise in log-odds than in probability, so link-scale Bayes factors could contradict the estimates. BF~10~ > 3 indicates moderate, BF~10~ > 10 strong, BF~10~ > 30 very strong, and BF~10~ > 100 extreme evidence for a difference, and BF~01~ = 1/BF~10~ the corresponding evidence for no difference; values between 1/3 and 3 are anecdotal [@leewagenmakers2014]. Because a Bayes factor depends on the prior, all comparisons between conditions received the same prior, and we report how sensitive the posteriors were to the priors [power-scaling sensitivity; @priorsense2023].

### Deviations From the Preregistration

Deviations from the preregistration, the reasons for them, and their likely effect on the results are listed in @apx-c (@tbl-deviations).

```{r}
#| label: claims-check
#| include: false
# The Results text below makes some interpretive statements in words (e.g., "as
# predicted", "no general benefit"). The numbers update automatically when the data or
# models change, but the words do not. Each statement is checked here; if the data no
# longer support it, rendering stops with a message saying which sentence to revise.
claim <- function(ok, text) if (!isTRUE(ok)) stop("Revise the Results text: ", text, call. = FALSE)
gen_bf01 <- \(mod, par = "mu") BY_row(mod, "Non-prequestioned", par = par)$BF01

claim(all(preq_by_cond$pre_m < 0.25), "prequestions: 'participants knew little of the material before reading'")
claim(pq_row$pd < 0.95 && abs(pq_row$est) < 5, "prequestions: scores described as similar in the two conditions")
# final test
claim(B_pos("final_test", "Prequestioned"),
      "final test: specific benefit described as present, with strong evidence")
# general effect on the final test: present by the pd rule (pd > 97.5%) when negative (a cost);
# the text reports no general benefit; a cost by the pd rule is reported in Results only
ft_gen <- BY_row("final_test", "Non-prequestioned")
gen_cost <- ft_gen$est < 0 && ft_gen$pd > 0.975
claim(ft_gen$pd < 0.975 || gen_cost, "final test: a general *benefit* would need new text")
claim(ft_gen$BF10 < 3,
      "abstract, Discussion: 'no general benefit' and no general cost interpreted")
claim(GT_row("final_test", "Polio")$lo > 0 && GT_row("final_test", "TB")$hi < 0 && GT_pos("final_test", "Interaction"),
      "final test, Group x Topic: each prequestion group scored relatively higher on its own topic (crossover)")
# eye movements, pooled
claim(B_pos("total_fix", "Prequestioned", par = "tau"),
      "eye movements: prequestioned sentences have a longer tail (τ)")
claim(BY_row("total_fix", "Prequestioned", par = "mu")$BF01 > 3,
      "eye movements: evidence that typical reading time (μ) did not change")
claim(B_pos("regressed_in", "Prequestioned"),
      "eye movements: readers more likely to return to prequestioned sentences")
claim(B_pos("reread_time", "Prequestioned"),
      "eye movements: prequestioned sentences re-read for longer once readers returned")
claim(BY_row("first_pass", "Prequestioned", par = "mu")$BF01 > 3,
      "eye movements: typical right-bounded (first-pass) reading time (μ) did not change")
claim(B_pos("first_pass", "Prequestioned", par = "tau"),
      "eye movements: longer tail (τ) already in right-bounded (first-pass) reading")
gen_keys <- list(c("first_pass", "mu"), c("first_pass", "tau"), c("total_fix", "mu"),
                 c("total_fix", "tau"), c("regressed_in", "mu"), c("reread_time", "mu"))
gen_bfs <- map_dbl(gen_keys, \(k) gen_bf01(k[1], k[2]))
gen_pds <- map_dbl(gen_keys, \(k) BY_row(k[1], "Non-prequestioned", par = k[2])$pd)
# Group x Topic: the late effects (look-backs, re-reading) came mainly from the TB group
tm <- \(mod, grp, tp) filter(bayes$means_topic, model == mod, parameter == "mu", condition == grp, topic == tp)$Mean
for (m in c("regressed_in", "reread_time")) {
  claim((tm(m, "TB", "TB") - tm(m, "Control", "TB")) > 2 * abs(tm(m, "Polio", "Polio") - tm(m, "Control", "Polio")),
        paste("Group x Topic:", m, "effect described as coming mainly from the TB group"))
}
claim(all(gen_bfs > 1) && all(gen_pds < 0.975),
      "eye movements: no general effect on any measure; Bayes factors favour its absence")

```

# Results

## Prequestion Performance

As intended, participants knew little of the material before reading. Participants in the Polio prequestion condition earned `r PQ("Polio", "pre_m")` of the available points on the prequestions (*SD* = `r PQ("Polio", "pre_sd")`) and those in the TB prequestion condition `r PQ("TB", "pre_m")` (*SD* = `r PQ("TB", "pre_sd")`). Participants attempted `r PQ("Polio", "att_m")` (Polio) and `r PQ("TB", "att_m")` (TB) of the prequestions; the rest were left blank or answered "I don't know". In a beta-binomial model of the points earned on each prequestion, with random intercepts for participants and questions, prequestion scores were similar in the two conditions (model-estimated scores: `r PQB_mean("TB")` in the TB and `r PQB_mean("Polio")` in the Polio condition), `r PQB_diff`.

## Final Test Performance


Final test performance was analysed as the proportion of each question's points earned (@fig-test). Pooled over the two prequestion conditions, participants earned `r B_mean("final_test", "Prequestioned")` of the points on their prequestioned topic, compared with `r B_mean("final_test", "Control")` for no-prequestion participants on the same questions, a specific benefit of `r BY_txt("final_test", "Prequestioned")`: `r B_ev("final_test", "Prequestioned")` evidence for a difference. On the non-prequestioned topic they earned `r B_mean("final_test", "Non-prequestioned")`, `r if (gen_cost) "numerically slightly lower than in the no-prequestion condition" else "which did not reliably differ from the no-prequestion condition"`, `r BY_txt("final_test", "Non-prequestioned")`.`r if (gen_cost) paste0(" There was therefore no general benefit. Although the difference met the preregistered criterion (pd > 97.5%) in the direction of a cost, the Bayes factor was inconclusive, providing only ", bf_strength(gen_bf01("final_test")), " evidence for no difference, so we do not interpret it as a general cost.") else paste0(" The Bayes factor provided ", bf_strength(gen_bf01("final_test")), " evidence for no difference, so there was no general benefit.")`

In the Group × Topic model (@fig-test; Bayes factors on the response scale, see Statistical Analysis), the Polio group scored higher on Polio than on TB questions (`r B_mean("final_test", "Polio", tp = "Polio")` vs. `r B_mean("final_test", "Polio", tp = "TB")`), Polio − TB = `r GT_txt("final_test", "Polio")`, whereas the TB group scored higher on TB than on Polio questions (`r B_mean("final_test", "TB", tp = "TB")` vs. `r B_mean("final_test", "TB", tp = "Polio")`), Polio − TB = `r GT_txt("final_test", "TB")`. The no-prequestion group, which saw no prequestions, scored `r B_mean("final_test", "Control", tp = "Polio")` on Polio and `r B_mean("final_test", "Control", tp = "TB")` on TB questions, Polio − TB = `r GT_txt("final_test", "Control")``r if (GT_row("final_test", "Control")$lo > 0 || GT_row("final_test", "Control")$hi < 0) ", a difference in difficulty between the two sets of questions" else ""`. The Group × Topic interaction contrast—the Polio group's Polio − TB difference minus the TB group's—was `r GT_txt("final_test", "Interaction")`: `r bf_strength(GT_row("final_test", "Interaction")$BF10)` evidence that each prequestion group did relatively better on its own topic.

```{r}
#| label: fig-test
#| fig-cap: "Final Test Performance: Posterior Distributions of the Model-Estimated Means"
#| apa-note: "Posterior distributions of the model-estimated proportion of a question's points earned, averaged over the observed sample. Left: the status model, pooled over the two prequestion groups and both topics (prequestioned, non-prequestioned, and no-prequestion). Other panels: the Group × Topic model, for the Polio and TB questions in the Polio, TB, and no-prequestion groups; colours give the status of the questions for the readers in that group. Preq. = prequestioned; non-preq. = non-prequestioned; no-preq. = no-prequestion. Points are posterior means; thick and thin bars are 66% and 95% credible intervals."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
post_plot("final_test", c(final_test = "Final test score (%)"), "questions")
```

## Eye Movements

Without prequestions, readers spent on average `r num(rt_desc$total_m)` ms per word on a target sentence in total (*SD* = `r num(rt_desc$total_sd)`; about `r num(60000 / rt_desc$total_m)` words per minute), `r num(rt_desc$srp_m)` ms per word (*SD* = `r num(rt_desc$srp_sd)`) of it in first-pass reading (selective regression-path duration). The ex-Gaussian estimates below divide such reading times into a typical part (μ) and a tail (τ), which sum to the mean. We first compare prequestioned and non-prequestioned sentences with the same sentences read by no-prequestion readers (@tbl-status), and then test the preregistered Group × Topic crossover (@fig-eye). @fig-eye shows the posterior distributions of the means for every measure, pooled and by group.

### Prequestioned and Non-Prequestioned Sentences Versus the No-Prequestion Condition

Prequestions changed how readers read the sentences that answered them, compared with no-prequestion readers reading the same sentences (@tbl-status). During first-pass reading, measured as selective regression-path duration, typical reading time did not differ, μ: `r BY_txt("first_pass", "Prequestioned", par = "mu")`, with `r bf_strength(BY_row("first_pass", "Prequestioned", par = "mu")$BF10)` evidence for no difference. The tail of unusually long first-pass readings, however, was longer for prequestioned sentences, τ: `r BY_txt("first_pass", "Prequestioned", par = "tau")`, although the Bayes factor provided only `r B_ev("first_pass", "Prequestioned", par = "tau")` evidence for a difference. Total gaze duration showed the same pattern more clearly: prequestioned sentences had a longer tail, τ: `r BY_txt("total_fix", "Prequestioned", par = "tau")`, `r B_ev("total_fix", "Prequestioned", par = "tau")` evidence for a difference, whereas typical reading time did not differ, μ: `r BY_txt("total_fix", "Prequestioned", par = "mu")`, with `r bf_strength(BY_row("total_fix", "Prequestioned", par = "mu")$BF10)` evidence for no difference. After moving on, readers were more likely to return to prequestioned sentences from later text (`r B_mean("regressed_in", "Prequestioned")` vs. `r B_mean("regressed_in", "Control")`), `r BY_txt("regressed_in", "Prequestioned")`, `r B_ev("regressed_in", "Prequestioned")` evidence, and when they returned, they re-read prequestioned sentences for longer (`r B_mean("reread_time", "Prequestioned")` vs. `r B_mean("reread_time", "Control")`), `r BY_txt("reread_time", "Prequestioned")`, `r B_ev("reread_time", "Prequestioned")` evidence.

Non-prequestioned sentences, by contrast, were read like the same sentences in the no-prequestion condition. No measure showed a general effect (non-prequestioned − no-prequestion, @tbl-status; all pd < 97.5%), and on every measure the Bayes factor favoured its absence (BF~01~ from `r fmt_num(min(gen_bfs), 1)` to `r fmt_num(max(gen_bfs), 1)`), with `r if (all(gen_bfs > 3)) "moderate or stronger evidence on every measure" else sprintf("moderate or stronger evidence for %d of the %d measures and anecdotal evidence for the rest", sum(gen_bfs > 3), length(gen_bfs))`. The effects of prequestions on reading were therefore specific to the prequestioned sentences.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-status
#| tbl-cap: "Prequestioned and Non-Prequestioned Sentences Versus the Same Sentences Read Without Prequestions"
#| tbl-colwidths: [22, 21, 9, 9, 21, 9, 9]
#| apa-note: "Posterior means and 95% credible intervals of the differences, pooled over the Polio and TB prequestion conditions and averaged over the two topics, in ms per word (durations) or percentage points (regressions-in). Prequestioned − no-prequestion is the specific effect and non-prequestioned − no-prequestion the general effect of prequestions. Selective regression-path duration (first-pass reading) and total gaze duration were analysed with ex-Gaussian models (μ = typical reading time; τ = tail of unusually long readings); regressions-in with a logistic model; re-reading time, for sentences that were re-read, with a Gamma model. pd = probability of direction. BF~10~ = Bayes factor for a difference (Savage–Dickey); BF~01~ = 1/BF~10~, evidence for no difference. Selective regression-path duration is a local measure; all others are global."
eye_keys <- tribble(
  ~mod,           ~par,  ~Measure,
  "first_pass",   "mu",  "Selective regression path: μ",
  "first_pass",   "tau", "Selective regression path: τ",
  "total_fix",    "mu",  "Total gaze: μ",
  "total_fix",    "tau", "Total gaze: τ",
  "regressed_in", "mu",  "Regression-in",
  "reread_time",  "mu",  "Re-reading time")
ci_cell <- \(r) sprintf("%s [%s, %s]", fmt_num(r$est, 1), fmt_num(r$lo, 1), fmt_num(r$hi, 1))
pd_cell <- \(r) if (r$pd >= 0.9995) "> 99.9%" else paste0(fmt_num(100 * r$pd, 1), "%")
eye_keys |>
  mutate(spec = map2(mod, par, \(m, p) BY_row(m, "Prequestioned", par = p)),
         gen  = map2(mod, par, \(m, p) BY_row(m, "Non-prequestioned", par = p))) |>
  transmute(Measure,
            `Prequestioned − No-prequestion` = map_chr(spec, ci_cell),
            pd = map_chr(spec, pd_cell),
            `BF~10~` = map_chr(spec, \(r) fmt_BF(r$BF10)),
            `Non-prequestioned − No-prequestion` = map_chr(gen, ci_cell),
            `pd ` = map_chr(gen, pd_cell),
            `BF~01~` = map_chr(gen, \(r) fmt_BF(r$BF01))) |>
  knitr::kable(format = "pipe")
```

### Group × Topic

```{r}
#| label: topic-prep
#| include: false
# Interaction contrast for each eye-movement measure: present (pd > 95%) or not
int_status <- eye_keys |>
  mutate(status = map2_chr(mod, par, \(m, p)
    if (GT_pos(m, "Interaction", p)) "pos" else "no"))
nice <- c(`Selective regression path: μ` = "typical first-pass reading time (μ)",
          `Selective regression path: τ` = "the tail of first-pass reading (τ)",
          `Total gaze: μ` = "typical total reading time (μ)",
          `Total gaze: τ` = "the tail of total reading time (τ)",
          `Regression-in` = "look-backs from later text", `Re-reading time` = "re-reading time")
# measures with the given status; with numbers = TRUE, each with its interaction estimate
int_list <- function(st, numbers = FALSE) {
  r <- filter(int_status, status == st)
  lab <- nice[r$Measure]
  if (numbers) lab <- sprintf("%s: %s", lab, map2_chr(r$mod, r$par, \(m, p) GT_txt(m, "Interaction", p)))
  knitr::combine_words(lab, sep = if (numbers) "; " else ", ")
}
int_summary_fun <- function(numbers) {
  parts <- c(
    if (any(int_status$status == "pos")) paste("positive (pd > 95%) for", int_list("pos", numbers)),
    if (any(int_status$status == "no")) paste("not reliably positive for", int_list("no", numbers)))
  n <- length(parts)
  if (n == 1) parts
  else if (numbers) paste(parts, collapse = ". It was ")     # two sentences
  else paste0(paste(parts[-n], collapse = "; "), "; and ", parts[n])
}
int_summary <- int_summary_fun(FALSE)          # Discussion
int_summary_num <- int_summary_fun(TRUE)       # Results, with the estimates
```

The preregistered prediction was a crossover: longer reading of Polio than of TB sentences in the Polio group, the reverse in the TB group, and no difference in the no-prequestion group, so that the Group × Topic interaction contrast would be positive. The interaction contrast was `r int_summary_num`. For the tail of total gaze duration (τ), the Polio − TB difference was `r GT_txt("total_fix", "Polio", "tau")` in the Polio group, `r GT_txt("total_fix", "TB", "tau")` in the TB group, and `r GT_txt("total_fix", "Control", "tau")` in the no-prequestion group. For look-backs from later text (Bayes factors on the response scale), it was `r GT_txt("regressed_in", "Polio")` in the Polio group, `r GT_txt("regressed_in", "TB")` in the TB group, and `r GT_txt("regressed_in", "Control")` in the no-prequestion group. For re-reading time, it was `r GT_txt("reread_time", "Polio")` in the Polio group, `r GT_txt("reread_time", "TB")` in the TB group, and `r GT_txt("reread_time", "Control")` in the no-prequestion group. Because the Polio and TB sentences differ, the no-prequestion group shows how the topics are read without prequestions (@fig-eye). Compared with that group, the crossover in look-backs came mainly from the TB group, who looked back to TB sentences more often (`r B_mean("regressed_in", "TB", tp = "TB")` vs. `r B_mean("regressed_in", "Control", tp = "TB")`) and to Polio sentences less often (`r B_mean("regressed_in", "TB", tp = "Polio")` vs. `r B_mean("regressed_in", "Control", tp = "Polio")`) than no-prequestion readers, whereas the Polio group's look-backs differed little from those of no-prequestion readers on either topic (Polio: `r B_mean("regressed_in", "Polio", tp = "Polio")` vs. `r B_mean("regressed_in", "Control", tp = "Polio")`; TB: `r B_mean("regressed_in", "Polio", tp = "TB")` vs. `r B_mean("regressed_in", "Control", tp = "TB")`).
