Re-reading time showed the same asymmetry: the TB group re-read TB sentences for longer than no-prequestion readers (`r B_mean("reread_time", "TB", tp = "TB")` vs. `r B_mean("reread_time", "Control", tp = "TB")`), whereas the Polio group's re-reading of Polio sentences was closer to that of no-prequestion readers (`r B_mean("reread_time", "Polio", tp = "Polio")` vs. `r B_mean("reread_time", "Control", tp = "Polio")`). These comparisons across groups are descriptive.

```{r}
#| label: fig-eye
#| fig-cap: "Eye-Movement Measures: Posterior Distributions of the Model-Estimated Means"
#| apa-note: "Posterior distributions of the model-estimated means, averaged over the observed sample. For the ex-Gaussian measures, μ and τ are shown separately; a mean reading time is μ + τ. Left: the status models, pooled over the two prequestion groups and both topics (prequestioned, non-prequestioned, and no-prequestion sentences). Other panels: the Group × Topic models, for the Polio and TB sentences in the Polio, TB, and no-prequestion groups; colours give the status of the sentences for the readers in that group. μ and τ are the Gaussian mean (typical reading time) and the tail mean (unusually long readings) of the ex-Gaussian models of selective regression-path duration (first-pass reading) and total gaze duration. Durations are in ms per word; regressions-in are the percentage of sentences returned to from later text; re-reading time is for sentences that were re-read. Preq. = prequestioned; non-preq. = non-prequestioned; no-preq. = no-prequestion. Points are posterior means; thick and thin bars are 66% and 95% credible intervals."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 10
post_plot(c("first_pass_mu", "first_pass_tau", "total_fix_mu", "total_fix_tau", "regressed_in",
            "reread_time"),
          c(first_pass_mu = "Selective regression\npath: μ (ms/word)", first_pass_tau = "Selective regression\npath: τ (ms/word)",
            total_fix_mu = "Total gaze: μ\n(ms/word)", total_fix_tau = "Total gaze: τ\n(ms/word)",
            regressed_in = "Regression-in\n(%)", reread_time = "Re-reading time\n(ms/word)"),
          "sentences")
```

# Discussion

This study used eye tracking to examine how prequestions influence the allocation of visual attention during reading and whether these changes are associated with subsequent memory benefits. On the final test, prequestions produced the expected specific benefit, with no reliable general benefit. Participants performed better on information related to their prequestioned topic, as reflected in the Group × Topic interaction (`r bf_strength(GT_row("final_test", "Interaction")$BF10)` evidence). Eye movements showed a similarly selective pattern. Compared with the same sentences read without prequestions, prequestioned sentences exhibited a greater contribution from unusually long reading times, including during first-pass reading. Readers also looked back to these sentences more frequently and spent more time rereading them after moving on to later material. In contrast, processing of non-prequestioned sentences did not reliably differ from the no-prequestion condition across the eye-movement measures. The Group × Topic interaction contrast for eye movements was `r int_summary` (@fig-eye). Together, these findings suggest that prequestions selectively alter how readers process information relevant to the questions, rather than producing a general increase in processing across the passage.

The distributional analyses provide further insight into the nature of these changes. Prequestions did not produce a reliable shift in the Gaussian component (μ) of reading times, with Bayes factors favoring the absence of a difference in both first-pass reading and total gaze duration. Instead, prequestions increased the exponential component (τ), indicating a greater contribution from unusually long reading times. This pattern suggests that prequestions do not uniformly slow reading of relevant information, but instead alter the distribution in a way consistent with additional processing on some encounters with an answer. The increased frequency of look-backs and longer rereading times further indicate that readers devoted additional processing to prequestioned information after initially encountering it. Importantly, these changes were specific to the prequestioned sentences, with no corresponding increase or decrease in processing of non-prequestioned sentences. This specificity parallels the meta-analytic findings of @kingshepard2025 and @sthilaire2023, who reported a robust specific memory benefit but neither a reliable general benefit nor a general cost. The absence of changes to non-prequestioned information also provides little support for accounts proposing that prequestions broadly increase attention or monitoring across an entire topic or passage. `r claim(BY_row("first_pass", "Prequestioned", par = "mu")$BF01 > 3 && BY_row("total_fix", "Prequestioned", par = "mu")$BF01 > 3, "Discussion: Bayes factors favour no difference in μ, in first-pass reading and total gaze duration")`

One possible explanation for this pattern is that additional processing is triggered when readers recognize that a sentence contains the answer to a prequestion. @lewis2012 proposed a related mechanism in which information that overlaps with a prequestion in wording or meaning "resonates" with the reader's memory of the question, prompting additional inspection. Such recognition may occur only after readers have processed enough of a sentence to identify its relevance. Moreover, recognition may not occur on every encounter, particularly if readers fail to notice the connection or no longer remember the question. Consequently, recognition-triggered processing could produce disproportionately long reading times on some occasions rather than a uniform increase in reading duration. This interpretation is consistent with the increased τ observed in the present study. Previous distributional research has similarly shown that some experimental manipulations primarily affect the right tail of response-time distributions rather than their location. For example, modest visual degradation of text has been found to shift μ [@white2012], whereas familiarity in scene viewing has been associated with increases in τ [@guy2020]. Although these distributional patterns do not uniquely identify cognitive processes, our findings are consistent with the possibility that recognizing question-relevant information sometimes triggers additional processing.

The timing of the eye-movement effects provides further insight into this possibility. The increase in τ during first-pass reading suggests that additional processing can occur during the initial encounter with an answer, before readers move on to subsequent text. At the same time, the greater frequency of look-backs and longer rereading times suggest that readers also return to relevant information after initially encountering it. These returns may provide opportunities to compare the information with the original prequestion or an earlier guess, resolve uncertainty, or rehearse the answer. Recognition of the connection between a prequestion and its answer may therefore play an important role in determining when readers allocate additional attention. Consistent with the importance of remembering prequestions, @sthilaire2020 found that prequestions enhanced learning from video lectures only when learners remembered the questions. The present findings are also relevant to the attentional-window account [@sana2023], which proposes that attention remains elevated while learners search for an answer and returns to baseline once the answer is found. Although this account can accommodate increased processing while readers search for relevant information, it does not straightforwardly predict the additional look-backs and rereading observed after readers have already encountered the answer. These findings suggest that the influence of prequestions on visual processing may extend beyond the initial search for relevant information.

More broadly, the results suggest that the benefits of prequestions cannot be explained simply in terms of increased time spent attending to relevant information. If prequestions produced a uniform slowing of reading, we might expect a broader shift in reading-time distributions. Instead, the observed effects were concentrated in the right tail and in subsequent returns to the targeted sentences. This pattern is consistent with the possibility that prequestions influence the processing of relevant information after it has been recognized, rather than merely encouraging readers to allocate more attention to it in advance. Such an interpretation aligns with the *mental model hypothesis* proposed by @motz2026, according to which prequestions activate relevant prior knowledge that facilitates the processing of related information during learning. On this account, recognizing a connection between incoming information and previously activated knowledge may prompt additional attention or elaboration. However, the present study cannot determine whether such knowledge activation preceded the observed changes in eye movements. Furthermore, because the non-prequestioned sentences concerned a different disease, the design cannot establish whether activated knowledge would also facilitate processing of related but non-prequestioned information within the same topic.

The observed pattern is also compatible with metacognitive explanations of the prequestion effect. By revealing gaps in learners' knowledge, prequestions may encourage monitoring for relevant information during subsequent learning [@kingshepard2025]. Recognizing that a sentence provides an answer may prompt learners to evaluate their earlier responses or attend more closely to information they previously could not retrieve. The longer readings and additional returns observed here are consistent with such monitoring, although eye movements alone cannot distinguish metacognitive evaluation from elaboration, rehearsal, or other forms of additional processing. Future research combining eye tracking with measures such as judgments of learning or confidence ratings may help differentiate these possibilities [@kingshepard2025]. Importantly, the present findings also do not establish that increased processing causes the specific memory benefit. Because reading behavior was measured rather than experimentally manipulated, the relationship between additional processing and subsequent memory remains correlational. Prequestions may also strengthen memory through processes that are not directly reflected in eye movements. Experiments that manipulate opportunities for rereading or returning to previously encountered answers could help determine whether these behaviors contribute causally to the prequestion effect.

The present findings also extend previous eye-tracking research on prequestions. Because participants in our TB prequestion condition read the same passage used in Experiment 2 of @lewis2012 and received prequestions about the same topic, comparisons between the TB and no-prequestion groups provide a close conceptual replication of that experiment. Consistent with @lewis2012, TB prequestions improved subsequent memory for TB information (`r tb_txt("final_test", "TB")`), increased the frequency of look-backs to TB sentences (`r tb_txt("regressed_in", "TB")`), and increased the time spent rereading those sentences (`r tb_txt("reread_time", "TB")`). However, whereas @lewis2012 found more re-inspection of targeted sentences during first-pass reading, we found no reliable difference in first-pass reading of TB sentences when examining either μ (`r tb_txt("first_pass", "TB")`) or τ (`r tb_txt("first_pass", "TB", "tau")`). When data were pooled across both prequestion groups, first-pass reading showed an increase in τ without a corresponding shift in μ, although the evidence was weak. `r claim(tb_row("final_test", "TB")$lo > 0 && tb_row("regressed_in", "TB")$lo > 0 && tb_row("reread_time", "TB")$lo > 0 && tb_row("first_pass", "TB")$lo < 0 && tb_row("first_pass", "TB", "tau")$lo < 0, "Discussion: comparison of the TB group with Lewis and Mensink (2012)")`

Several methodological differences may contribute to the discrepancies between studies. The present study included a larger sample and counterbalanced the targeted content, allowing us to compare reading of the same sentences with and without prequestions. We also measured rereading as time spent on a sentence after the reader had progressed beyond it, and operationalized first-pass processing using selective regression-path duration [@schotter2025]. This measure was particularly useful because approximately half of first passes were interrupted by brief returns to the preceding line. In addition, the distributional analyses allowed us to distinguish changes in the Gaussian and exponential components of reading times, which cannot be separated through analyses of means alone. This distinction is important because a difference in average reading time can arise from different changes in the underlying distribution, with potentially different implications for how prequestions influence reading.

Our findings also resemble those of @bostan2026, who observed more fixations on prequestioned sentences and more transitions between them. These patterns are broadly consistent with the increased look-backs and rereading observed here. However, unlike the present study and much of the prequestion literature, @bostan2026 also reported a general memory benefit. One possible explanation concerns the types of prequestions used. Their integrative questions required readers to combine information distributed across different parts of the passage, potentially encouraging processing of information beyond the sentences directly targeted by the questions [@pan2023]. In contrast, the prequestions used in the present study targeted individual facts contained within single sentences, and neither memory nor eye movements showed reliable general benefits. This difference is consistent with the possibility that the scope of attentional processing depends on the information required to answer the prequestions. However, given the relatively small sample in @bostan2026 (12 participants per group), this explanation remains tentative.

More broadly, these findings highlight the importance of selecting appropriate statistical analyses when examining eye-tracking data. Reading-time distributions are typically right-skewed, and experimental manipulations may affect different parts of these distributions in different ways. Conventional analyses of mean reading times can identify overall differences between conditions but cannot distinguish a general shift in reading times from a change in the right tail of the distribution. In the present study, the ex-Gaussian analyses revealed that prequestions increased the exponential component (τ) of reading times without a corresponding shift in the Gaussian component (μ). This distinction would not have been apparent from analyses of means alone. Thus, distributional analyses can provide a more detailed characterization of how experimental manipulations influence reading behavior, revealing patterns that may otherwise be overlooked or obscured by conventional approaches.

One limitation of the present study concerns the characteristics of the reading materials. Each topic was represented by only five target sentences and five final-test questions. Moreover, the Polio and TB sentences differed in length, reading difficulty, content, and position within the passage.irst, each topic was represented by only five target sentences and five final-test questions. Moreover, the Polio and TB sentences differed in length, reading difficulty, content, and position within the passage. These differences are particularly important in eye-tracking research, where linguistic and visual characteristics of the text can influence fixation durations, regressions, and rereading independently of the experimental manipulation. Consequently, differences in eye movements between topics cannot necessarily be attributed to prequestions alone. To address this concern, our primary analyses compared the same sentences across conditions, allowing us to account for fixed characteristics of the sentences themselves. Nevertheless, the effects were not identical across topics. In particular, increases in look-backs and rereading were driven primarily by the TB prequestion group, whose target sentences also attracted more look-backs in the no-prequestion condition. These findings underscore the importance of carefully controlling text stimuli in eye-tracking research. Future studies should more closely match target sentences on relevant linguistic and visual characteristics, including sentence length, syntactic complexity, reading difficulty, and position within the passage, or systematically counterbalance which sentences are targeted by prequestions across versions of the same text.

In summary, prequestions selectively changed how readers processed information that answered the questions. Rather than producing a uniform slowing of reading, prequestions increased the contribution of unusually long reading times and prompted readers to return to relevant information more frequently and for longer periods. These effects were restricted to prequestioned sentences and accompanied a specific memory benefit, with no reliable general benefit. The pattern is consistent with the possibility that recognizing information as relevant to a prequestion triggers additional processing during initial reading and subsequent rereading. However, whether such processing contributes causally to improved memory, or instead accompanies other learning mechanisms initiated by prequestions, remains an open question.


# Questions and Scoring Rules {#apx-a}

Prequestion and final test responses were scored with the same rule-based script (`scoring_rubric.R`), written by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic; model ID `claude-opus-5-5`) and applied identically to every response. Each question awarded one point per correct element present in the response (@tbl-questions, @tbl-scoring). Blank responses, "I don't know" and similar responses, and random keystrokes scored 0. Minor misspellings were accepted when the intended word was unambiguous (e.g., "afganistan"). The same rules were used for the prequestions and the final test.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-questions
#| tbl-cap: "Final Test Questions and Answers"
#| tbl-colwidths: [5, 8, 45, 34, 8]
#| apa-note: "Points = maximum points for the question. The Polio prequestion condition answered questions 1–4 and 10 before reading; the TB prequestion condition answered questions 5–9."
answer_key |>
  arrange(questnum) |>
  transmute(Q = questnum, Topic = Condition, Question, Answer, Points) |>
  knitr::kable(format = "pipe")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-scoring
#| tbl-cap: "Scoring Rules and Agreement With the Second Rater for Each Question"
#| tbl-colwidths: [5, 63, 8, 12, 12]
#| apa-note: "One point was awarded for each credited element present in a response, up to the question's maximum (see Table A1). *n* = number of non-blank responses (prequestions and final test) scored by both the automated rubric and the second rater; Exact = percentage of responses given the same score; ICC = ICC(2,1), absolute agreement."
credited <- c(
  `1`  = "The number 17 (as a whole number, e.g., not 170).",
  `2`  = "A negative answer: \"no\", \"no cure\", or \"not a cure\".",
  `3`  = "One point each for Nigeria, India, Pakistan, and Afghanistan.",
  `4`  = "One point each for antibiotics; analgesics or pain relief; exercise (including physical activity or therapy); and diet or nutrition. \"Antibiotic resistance\" alone was not credited.",
  `5`  = "One point each for cough (or blood-tinged sputum/phlegm); fever (or temperature); sweats (including night sweats); and weight loss.",
  `6`  = "10% (or \"ten percent\", 1/10); not credited if stated as \"less than\" or \"under\" 10%.",
  `7`  = "One point each for antibiotics (or antibacterials); two (two drugs, courses, rounds, or types); and long-term (long, extended, prolonged, or months).",
  `8`  = "A negative answer (\"no\").",
  `9`  = "One point each for cough, sneeze, and spit (or saliva).",
  `10` = "One point each for a starting value of hundreds of thousands (100,000–999,999) and an end value of about a thousand (500–9,999, or \"a thousand\")."
)
tibble(Q = 1:10, `Credited elements` = credited[as.character(1:10)]) |>
  left_join(transmute(rater$by_question, Q = as.integer(questnum), `*n*` = n,
                      Exact = paste0(fmt_num(100 * exact, 1), "%"),
                      ICC = sub("^0", "", fmt_num(icc, 2))), by = "Q") |>
  knitr::kable(format = "pipe")
```

# Model Specifications {#apx-b}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-models
#| tbl-cap: "Bayesian Models: Families, Effects, and Priors"
#| tbl-colwidths: [20, 22, 30, 28]
#| apa-note: "Pooled models: Status (prequestioned, non-prequestioned, no-prequestion) + Topic; Group × Topic models: Group (Polio, TB, no-prequestion) × Topic. Status, Condition, and Topic were coded with equal-prior contrasts, so the prior on the coefficients is also the prior on every pairwise difference between conditions (on the link scale). Other priors: intercepts normal(−1.5, 1) on the log scale (Gamma models; about 0.2 s per word), normal(0, 1.5) on the log-odds scale, and normal(0.2, 0.2) s per word for μ; ex-Gaussian σ and τ intercepts normal(−2.5, 1) on the softplus scale; random-effect *SD*s Student-*t*(3, 0, *v*) with *v* = 0.5 (Gamma models, ex-Gaussian σ and τ), 1 (logistic and beta-binomial models), or 0.1 (ex-Gaussian μ); random-effect correlations LKJ(2); the Gamma shape gamma(2, 0.5); beta-binomial overdispersion exponential(0.1). Durations were modelled in s per word."
s_tab <- bayes$settings
tribble(
  ~Measure, ~Family, ~`Random effects`, ~`Prior on comparisons`,
  "Total gaze duration", "Ex-Gaussian (μ identity; σ, τ softplus)",
  "μ and τ: participants (intercept, Topic slope), sentences (intercept, Status or Group slope); σ: participants (intercept)",
  sprintf("μ: normal(0, %s) s/word; τ: normal(0, %s)", s_tab$s_mu, s_tab$s_log),
  "Selective regression-path duration", "Ex-Gaussian (μ identity; σ, τ softplus)",
  "μ and τ: participants (intercept, Topic slope), sentences (intercept, Status or Group slope); σ: participants (intercept)",
  sprintf("μ: normal(0, %s) s/word; τ: normal(0, %s)", s_tab$s_mu, s_tab$s_log),
  "Re-reading time", "Gamma (log)",
  "Participants (intercept, Topic slope), sentences (intercept, Status or Group slope)",
  sprintf("normal(0, %s)", s_tab$s_log),
  "Regression-in (look-back)", "Bernoulli (logit)", "Participants (intercept, Topic slope), sentences (intercept, Status or Group slope)",
  sprintf("normal(0, %s)", s_tab$s_logit),
  "Final test", "Beta-binomial (logit)", "Participants (intercept, Topic slope), questions (intercept, Status or Group slope)",
  sprintf("normal(0, %s)", s_tab$s_logit),
  "Prequestions", "Beta-binomial (logit)", "Participants (intercept), questions (intercept)",
  sprintf("normal(0, %s)", s_tab$s_logit)
) |>
  knitr::kable(format = "pipe")
```

# Drift Correction {#apx-d}

Each fixation was assigned to a text line after correcting for vertical drift, separately for each reader and page. The correction combines two approaches used in automated drift-correction algorithms [@carr2022]: assigning sequences of fixations to a line together, and modelling drift as a function of position on the page. First, a single vertical offset was estimated: candidate shifts of the recorded positions were tried in steps of 0.05 line spacings, and the shift that minimized the summed squared distance between each fixation and its nearest text line was kept (distances were capped at one line spacing, so that stray fixations in the margins had little influence). Second, consecutive fixations moving along a line were grouped into chains; a chain ended at a horizontal jump larger than 10% of the screen width (e.g., a return sweep to the next line) or a vertical jump larger than 0.6 line spacings. Each chain was assigned as a whole to the text line nearest its median position, so that a single fixation drifting toward a neighbouring line stayed on the line being read. Third, because drift often grew down the page or across it, a linear model of the recorded vertical position as a function of the assigned line's position and the fixation's horizontal position (recorded *y* = *a* + *b* × line *y* + *c* × *x*) was fitted to fixations whose chain lay within half a line spacing of its line; gaze positions were corrected by inverting this model and the chains were reassigned, and this was repeated five times. The linear model was used only if it was plausible (a vertical stretch within 20% and a tilt of less than one line across the screen); otherwise the single offset was kept. Throughout, the correction was limited everywhere on the page to the calibration accuracy criterion of 0.5° (`r num(max_shift_cm, 2)` cm, about 0.45 of a line spacing), so it could not move a reader's gaze by a whole line. Chains more than half a line spacing from every text line were treated as off the text.
